concepts.title: Major Plant Groups
concepts.contentHtml:
Plants colonized land ~470 million years ago. Today's land plants fall into four main groups:

• Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts) — non-vascular; small, depend on water for fertilization.
• Pteridophytes (ferns, horsetails) — vascular but seedless.
• Gymnosperms (conifers, cycads, ginkgos) — seed plants without flowers.
• Angiosperms (flowering plants) — seed plants with flowers and fruits.

Angiosperms dominate today: ~300,000 species, vs ~1,000 gymnosperms, ~12,000 ferns, ~20,000 bryophytes (mosses and liverworts).

concepts.title: Why Land Plants Look So Different
concepts.contentHtml:
Moving onto land required solving several problems: water loss, mechanical support, gas exchange, fertilization without water, UV protection.

Cuticle (waxy outer layer) prevents desiccation. Stomata (controllable pores) allow gas exchange while limiting water loss. Lignin in cell walls provides mechanical support and water-conducting tubes (xylem). Pollen replaces motile sperm — no water needed.

Each major innovation defined a new plant group. Land plants are an evolutionary tour de force.

concepts.title: Why So Many Flowering Plants?
concepts.contentHtml:
Flowering plants exploded in diversity ~140 million years ago. Several reasons proposed:

• Coevolution with pollinators: insects, then birds and mammals.
• Faster life cycles: many angiosperms reproduce in months, not years.
• Fruits: animal-mediated seed dispersal gets seeds to new habitats.
• More efficient water transport: vessel elements in xylem (vs. tracheids in gymnosperms).

Angiosperms now account for >90% of plant species. Without them, no fruit, no grass, no most vegetables.

title: Photosynthesis
description: How plants make food from sunlight

concepts.title: The Big Picture
concepts.contentHtml:
Photosynthesis converts CO₂ + H₂O + light → glucose + O₂. The net equation looks simple; the molecular machinery is intricate.

Two stages: light-dependent reactions (in thylakoid membranes — split water, generate ATP and NADPH) and Calvin cycle (in stroma — fix CO₂ into sugar using ATP and NADPH).

Globally photosynthesis fixes ~120 Gt of carbon per year. About half on land, half in oceans (mostly cyanobacteria and eukaryotic algae).

concepts.title: The Light Reactions
concepts.contentHtml:
Photosystems I and II contain chlorophyll molecules that absorb light. Energy transfers through the antenna complex to a reaction center, where it splits water (PSII) and reduces NADP+ to NADPH (PSI).

The oxygen-evolving complex in PSII oxidizes water — producing the O₂ we breathe. This single chemical step transformed Earth's atmosphere ~2.4 billion years ago (the Great Oxidation Event).

The proton gradient generated drives ATP synthase, just like in mitochondria. Same physics, opposite direction.

concepts.title: C3, C4, and CAM
concepts.contentHtml:
The Calvin cycle's first enzyme, RuBisCO, sometimes mis-fixes O₂ instead of CO₂ (photorespiration). At high temperatures and low CO₂, photorespiration wastes ~30% of fixed carbon.

C4 plants (corn, sugarcane, many tropical grasses) concentrate CO₂ around RuBisCO, suppressing photorespiration. Higher yields in hot climates.

CAM plants (cacti, pineapple) open stomata at night, fix CO₂ as malate, then process it during the day with stomata closed — minimizing water loss.

About 3% of plant species are C4 but they dominate hot grasslands and major crops.

concepts.title: Vascular Tissues
concepts.contentHtml:
Vascular plants have two transport systems running through them:

Xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals upward from roots, driven mostly by transpiration pull (water evaporating from leaves draws more up). Made of dead cells with lignified walls — providing structural support too.

Phloem transports sugars from photosynthetic sources (mostly leaves) to sinks (roots, fruits, growing tips). Driven by pressure flow — sugars loaded at sources, water follows osmotically, the resulting pressure pushes sap to sinks.

concepts.title: Roots, Stems, Leaves
concepts.contentHtml:
Roots anchor and absorb water and nutrients. Root hairs dramatically increase surface area. Mycorrhizal fungi extend the absorptive reach further still.

Stems support the plant and conduct between roots and leaves. Modified stems include tubers (potato), runners (strawberry), and tendrils.

Leaves are the main photosynthetic organs. Stomata on the underside (mostly) regulate gas exchange. Veins (xylem + phloem) deliver water and remove sugars. Leaf shape balances photosynthesis vs water loss.

concepts.title: Plant Hormones
concepts.contentHtml:
Plants don't have nervous systems but use chemical signals to coordinate growth and responses. Five classical hormones:

• Auxins (IAA): promote cell elongation, phototropism, gravitropism.
• Cytokinins: cell division, delay senescence.
• Gibberellins: stem elongation, seed germination.
• Abscisic acid (ABA): stress response, stomatal closure, dormancy.
• Ethylene: fruit ripening, leaf abscission.

Modern agriculture extensively uses synthetic versions — herbicides like 2,4-D mimic auxins to kill broadleaves; ethylene controls banana ripening during shipping.

concepts.title: Flowers
concepts.contentHtml:
A flower is an angiosperm's reproductive structure. Sepals protect the bud; petals attract pollinators; stamens (anther + filament) produce pollen; carpels (stigma + style + ovary) receive pollen and develop into fruits.

Most flowers are bisexual (both stamens and carpels). Some species separate male and female flowers on the same plant (monoecious — corn) or different plants (dioecious — willows, hollies).

concepts.title: Pollination Strategies
concepts.contentHtml:
Pollen must reach a compatible stigma. Strategies include:

• Wind: grasses, oaks, pines. Cheap pollen produced in vast quantities; tiny grains; flowers reduced (no need to attract).
• Insects: most flowers; coevolved with bees, butterflies, flies. Petals, scents, and nectar attract.
• Birds: hummingbirds, sunbirds. Often red, tubular flowers with copious nectar.
• Bats, mammals: night-blooming flowers; agave, baobab.

Pollinator decline (especially honeybees and wild bees) is a major agricultural concern — about 75% of leading food crops benefit at least partly from animal (mostly insect) pollination.

concepts.title: Seeds & Fruits
concepts.contentHtml:
Fertilization produces a seed — embryo + nutrient store + protective coat. Seeds enabled colonization of dry land; they survive and disperse independently of the parent plant.

Surrounding tissue often becomes a fruit that aids dispersal: fleshy fruits attract animals (apples, berries); winged fruits ride wind (maple samaras); burrs hitch on fur; coconuts float.

Seed dormancy can last decades to centuries (sacred lotus seeds have germinated after ~1,300 years, a Judean date palm seed after ~2,000). The seed banks at Svalbard preserve crop genetic diversity for future generations.

title: Plants & Climate
description: Plants in the carbon cycle and global change

concepts.title: Plants in the Carbon Cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
Land plants fix ~60 Gt of carbon per year. Roughly half is respired back; the other half eventually returns to atmosphere via decomposition.

Forests store enormous stocks: roughly 800 Gt C in forests globally — comparable to atmospheric CO₂. Tropical rainforests are the densest carbon stores per area; boreal forests cover the largest area.

Deforestation releases carbon; reforestation captures it. But the carbon math depends on which forest, which place, and how it's managed.

concepts.title: Climate Change Effects
concepts.contentHtml:
Rising CO₂ enhances photosynthesis (some plants respond more than others; C4 plants benefit less since they already concentrate CO₂). Warmer temperatures extend growing seasons in some regions.

But increased drought, heat stress, and pest pressure already hurt productivity in many areas. Phenology is shifting — earlier springs, mismatches with pollinators.

Plants are both responding to climate change and shaping it. Their net feedback is one of the major uncertainties in climate models.

concepts.title: Crops, GMOs, and the Future
concepts.contentHtml:
Plant breeding and biotechnology drive agricultural yields. The Green Revolution (1940s-70s) doubled global wheat and rice yields through dwarf high-yield varieties. Borlaug's Nobel: 1970.

Modern GMO crops include Bt corn (insect resistance), Roundup-Ready soy (herbicide tolerance), Golden Rice (vitamin A biofortification). Adoption is widespread but politically contested.

CRISPR-edited plants are increasingly common. Climate-resilient crops, perennial grains (Kernza, a perennial wheatgrass), and improved photosynthesis (engineered C4 rice) are active research targets.
